source.title: Towards Generalizable and Efficient Large-Scale Generative Recommenders
source.authors: Qiu-Ling Xu; Ko-Jen Hsiao; Moumita Bhattacharya

record.tranche_reason: Tests task-dependent scaling of generative recommenders in recommendation, using validation MRR and an offset power-law fit rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: Relevant results are the three task-specific validation-MRR scaling fits and their fit-error comparisons, plus the production-shadow MRR comparisons. The analytical FLOPs estimates, latency replay, and MTP comparisons do not measure the claim versions selected here.
record.test_reason: It scales a generative recommender's backbone from 2M to 1B parameters on behavior-token sequences, holding data and evaluation fixed, and fits an offset power law to validation MRR per task. This tests whether the power-law form carries over to a non-text sequence-modelling setting (V5). The production-shadow comparison changes several components at once, so it is not a scale test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find scaling useful but uneven across tasks, propose task-specific offset scaling fits as a headroom diagnostic, and treat scale as one component alongside decoding cost, serving-latency alignment and item generalization.
record.recipe_differences: This is an industrial generative recommender study, not a language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling experiment. It fits offset power laws to validation MRR by backbone size, compares them with log-linear fits, and includes a production-shadow comparison whose model changes more than size.
record.method_sensitivity: Task category changes the fitted ceiling and fit-error improvement; the paper also notes that including embedding and decoding layers did not materially change task ordering or preference for the offset fit.

fits_no_version.finding: In a one-week shadow evaluation over 1M users, the 1B system beats the 2M baseline on MRR across Tasks A, B, C and cold-start (+22.5%, +11.3%, +7.4%, +28.1%). The systems also differ in decoding, objective and cold-start design.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaled production recommender systems, bundling scale with other changes, improve downstream production metrics.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the scaling fits or MRR comparisons. The production-shadow comparison changes backbone size, decoding, training objective, and cold-start design together, so it does not isolate the causal effect of scale. The task categories are anonymized, and raw pointwise MRR values are presented in a plot rather than a table.

untested.parts: No held-out extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Only parameter scaling of MRR is fitted. Data or compute scaling is not tested, and no loss-based fit is reported (test loss is mentioned only qualitatively).
Downstream-task predictability with scale or loss is not tested in a controlled way. The production shadow compares two models that are confounded by other changes.

Exponent or allocation dependence on parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method is not tested quantitatively. Only a qualitative statement is given that including embedding/decoding layers did not change task ordering.

missing.what: Per-size raw validation MRR points and the fitted exponent a and scale N0 for each task, needed to compare the power-law form with other studies.
Statement that test loss, Hit Rate and NDCG show similar qualitative scaling trends; no numbers are given.
Statement that counting embedding and decoding layers did not materially change task ordering or the preference for the offset fit; qualitative only.

record.verdict_notes: The record linked R1–R3 to V6/V7 and R4–R6 to V7. I re-linked these to V5, because the study tests whether a power-law form holds for a sequence model trained on non-text behavior data. The MRR is evaluated on the model's own time-split next-event prediction, not on separate downstream tasks, so it does not bear on V6. The offset-versus-log-linear comparison concerns the functional form, not disagreement between published laws, so it does not bear on V7. The shadow rows are confounded and are moved to fits_no_version. No uncertainty is reported for the fits.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No held-out extrapolation test compares predictions fitted on small runs with the observed losses of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or compute-optimal split is tested.
Architecture shape effects at fixed parameter count are not tested.
The study is in recommendation, but it does not test whether the same pretraining-loss power law holds across modalities or training regimes.

Tests validation MRR versus backbone size for recommendation tasks and reports a two-model production-shadow comparison. It does not test downstream performance as a function of language-model pretraining loss.

Compares offset and log-linear fits and reports task-specific ceilings. It does not vary parameter-count conventions, data, training schedules, or fitting procedures broadly, nor test how compute-optimal allocations depend on these choices.

rows.operation_detail: Varied backbone size while keeping training data, evaluation examples, test window, item vocabulary, embedding dimension, and decoding setup fixed; fitted an offset power law to validation MRR.
rows.measure: Validation MRR scaling fit; fitted saturation level P0
rows.note: The paper describes meaningful relative headroom for this task; raw MRR values by model size are shown in Figure 1.
rows.check: Bears on V5: the power-law form in a new domain, recommendation behavior sequences. It does not bear on V6, because MRR here is the model's own held-out next-event prediction on a time split, not a separate downstream task. P0 is a fitted parameter, not a measured value. The exponent a and N0 are not reported.

relationships.condition: Generative recommender, backbone 2M–1B parameters, validation MRR, Tasks A–C
relationships.reason: An offset power law fits all three tasks. It reduces RMSE against log-linear by 48.4%, 61.8% and 14.9% (R1–R6).
relationships.display_finding: An offset power law reduced RMSE relative to log-linear fits by 48.4%, 61.8% and 14.9% across the three tasks.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Generative recommender, backbone 2M–1B parameters, validation MRR, Tasks A–C
source_check.reason: R1–R6 report task-specific offset power laws and lower fit RMSE than log-linear fits across all three tasks.

relationships.condition: Task-dependent ceilings within 2M–1B (Tasks B and C)
relationships.reason: The power-law gains run into task-specific saturation levels. Task B's P0=0.604 is near its best observed MRR, and Task C's fit is the least precise (P0>1, smallest RMSE gain). Scale returns therefore depend on the task (R2, R3, R6).
relationships.display_finding: Task B's fitted ceiling of 0.604 was near its best observed MRR, while Task C had the least precise fit, a ceiling above 1 and the smallest RMSE improvement.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Task-dependent ceilings within 2M–1B (Tasks B and C)
source_check.reason: R2, R3 and R6 do not establish incomplete or failed power-law behavior. Task-dependent saturation is represented by the fitted offset power law itself; V5 does not require identical ceilings or marginal gains across tasks. Task C's estimated asymptote above 1 cautions against interpreting that estimate literally, but does not demonstrate failure of the scaling form.

tranche.reason: Controlled backbone-size sweeps and scaling-form comparisons test power-law behavior in the new setting of generative recommendation.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Section 3 isolates backbone scaling; Section 7's production-shadow comparison also changes decoding, objective and cold-start representations, so its gains cannot be attributed to scale alone.

statements.correction: Section 3: P(N)=P0-(N/N0)^(-a), a>0; task-specific fitted saturation levels. Task C P0=1.075; excess above MRR bound 1 attributed to estimation error. Table 2: offset fits outperform log-linear fits for every task; Task C RMSE reduction 14.9%. Supports V5 in the tested setting.
statements.problem: The task-dependent ceilings and Task C estimation error are accurately reported, but classifying this study as challenging V5 is unsupported. Neither demonstrates absent or reversed power-law scaling.
